Article Title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman: Within six months, ChatGPT could watch your screen, meetings and emails
Article Text:
Sam Altman (Getty images)

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman explains how ChatGPT could work in the coming days

“I think we are close to a world where you can have a descendant of ChatGPT watch your computer screen all the time, watch every meeting you're in, record every call, everything that has perfect context of your whole life, everything you see.

You choose what information you want it to have, but you can connect it to your texts or email or docs or Slack or whatever and then you have this thing that is not making decisions for you, but if you're the CEO of a startup, there's always more stuff to do than you can do and context you can't keep track of.

You can't read every piece of customer feedback every day. And you can just have this thing that's working alongside you, and as you're typing out a sales pitch to a customer or writing a strategy doc, it'll just say, ‘Hey, maybe here's another idea, or I think you're making a mistake here.

You should consider this, or I can do this thing for you to help.’

I think we're only one model generation away from this actually being incredibly useful. And I think that will change, hopefully at least for me, the way I work.”

ChatGPT memory and screen access

OpenAI's next step for AI assistants

Article Title: Snowflake announces dynamic model routing within Cortex AI Gateway and flagship products
Article Text: Snowflake has announced dynamic model routing within Cortex AI Gateway and Snowflake’s flagship AI products, alongside expanded access to leading open models. The new capabilities build on Cortex AI Gateway, which Snowflake announced in July 2026 as a unified foundation for governing agent connections, intelligently routing requests, and optimizing AI consumption. As companies deploy more AI apps and agents into production, using the same model for every task can drive up costs, while evaluating and managing a growing mix of models creates more work for development teams.With the addition of dynamic model routing, Cortex AI Gateway is claimed to automatically select the specific model with the optimal balance of quality and cost for the task at hand. Dynamic model routing is also integrated across Snowflake’s flagship AI products, including Snowflake CoCo and Snowflake CoWork, and is available to third-party AI agents using Cortex AI Gateway.In a press release, the company said that the new capability directs lower-complexity or repetitive tasks to more efficient models, while work that requires deeper reasoning is routed to frontier models. “This helps customers reduce unnecessary inference spend, without having to manage model selection for each request themselves,” it added.Snowflake will also be expanding customers’ access to leading open models, including DeepSeek-V4-Flash 07311and GLM-5.33, through Snowflake Cortex AI.This adds to Snowflake’s extensive model library, giving customers even more options to balance model quality and cost, while keeping governed data secure within Snowflake.Snowflake’s latest innovations give enterprises more control over the economics of AI as usage scales, helping them increase intelligence efficiency by matching each task with the right model and reducing unnecessary spend.“Enterprises are becoming much more rigorous about the economics of AI. The question is no longer how much AI they are using, but whether that AI is translating into meaningful business value,” said Sridhar Ramaswamy, CEO, Snowflake. “Achieving intelligence efficiency requires the flexibility to use the best model for each task as the landscape evolves. Snowflake’s role is to absorb that complexity so customers can focus on outcomes while we optimize model choice underneath. ”"Enterprises are drowning in model choices, but the real problem isn't which model to pick. It's the operational overhead of picking the right one for every task, at scale. Snowflake's dynamic model routing directly addresses that gap,” said Sanjeev Mohan, Principal and Founder, SanjMo. “By automating intelligent model selection within Cortex AI Gateway, Snowflake is removing a real friction point that has been slowing enterprise AI deployment. The ability to match workload complexity to model cost, without rebuilding your infrastructure every time a new model drops, is exactly the kind of efficiency enterprises need to move from AI experimentation to AI at scale."
Article Summary: Snowflake has added dynamic model routing to its Cortex AI Gateway and Snowflake CoCo products. Dynamic model routing is claimed to automatically select the specific model with the optimal balance of quality and cost for the task at hand. Snowflake will also be expanding customers’ access to leading open models.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: Real-time management: AI-powered platform planned to help track crowds, simulate scenarios & strengthen emergency response during Kumbh
Article Text:
Smart City corporation's command-and-control room, fully equipped and operational for the Kumbh Mela

Nashik

:





The Nashik-Trimbakeshwar Kumbh Mela Authority (NTKMA) will deploy an AI-powered “Digital Twin” platform for crowd control, mobility planning, emergency response, and disaster preparedness at the Simhastha Kumbh Mela 2027, strengthening technology-led event management.The proposed system will create a live digital replica of the Kumbh ecosystem by integrating GIS-based 2D and 3D maps with real-time operational data, surveillance feeds and AI analytics. Officials said the platform would serve as a decision-support tool, enabling authorities to monitor ground conditions, assess risks and coordinate multiple agencies involved in managing the event.Built on Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC), ‘Digital Twin’ will function as a unified dashboard for departments handling crowd management, traffic, sanitation, health services, security, disaster management and public amenities. “The platform will continuously process data from multiple sources to provide a real-time view of the Kumbh environment. Authorities will be able to track crowd density, analyse movement patterns, generate alerts and assess operational challenges as they emerge. It will also allow officials to simulate scenarios and evaluate response strategies before implementation,” an official said.Crowd intelligence and public safety are expected to be among its key applications.“By analysing pedestrian movement and crowd concentrations across bathing ghats, temples, roads and transit hubs, officials will be able to identify bottlenecks and prevent congestion during peak pilgrimage days,” the official said.It will also support transport planning by integrating traffic flows, public transport operations, parking facilities and pedestrian movement into a single digital framework. Officials said this would help improve diversion plans, optimise resource deployment and strengthen mobility management.Beyond crowd and traffic monitoring, 'Digital Twin’ will cover health services, emergency response, sanitation and waste management, utility services, environmental and river monitoring, weather-risk assessment and disaster preparedness. It will also assist in workforce deployment, lost-and-found operations and citizen support services.“The initiative is part of the proposed Maha Simhastha Kumbh AI Stack, which also includes an AI-first call centre, AI-powered lost-and-found services and ‘KumbhDoot’, an AI-based virtual assistant for pilgrims,” another official said.The digital ecosystem is proposed to be integrated with the Kumbh website and mobile application, offering crowd-density heat maps, route guidance, SOS support, weather alerts, traffic updates, parking information and public facility details.NTKMA commissioner Shekhar Singh said 'Digital Twin’ would operate on a “human-in-the-loop” model, with AI-generated insights supporting rather than replacing administrative decision-making. “It will operate on a human-in-the-loop model, with intelligent automation complemented by human oversight and validation. The objective is to use technology to strengthen the capacity of officials and field agencies to anticipate situations, assess alternatives and take timely decisions,” Singh said.With millions of pilgrims expected to attend Simhastha Kumbh Mela 2027, authorities believe the platform will improve safety, operational efficiency and service delivery while enabling more coordinated, data-driven management of one of the world’s largest religious gatherings.
Article Summary: The Nashik-Trimbakeshwar Kumbh Mela Authority (NTKMA) will deploy an AI-powered ‘Digital Twin’ platform for crowd control, mobility planning, emergency response, and disaster preparedness. The proposed system will integrate GIS- based 2D and 3D maps with real-time operational data, surveillance feeds and AI analytics.

Article Title: Idukki student assaulted by classmates for reporting drug use
Article Text:
AI image

Idukki

A 19-year-old student was allegedly brutally assaulted by three classmates at a hostel in Thodupuzha on Aug 11 after they learnt that he had informed teachers about their alleged drug use. The attack was so severe that one of his testicles had to be surgically removed.The student, a native of Anakkara, was pursuing a mobile phone and laptop servicing course at a private institution in Thodupuzha.According to a complaint filed by his father, the student noticed some hostel mates allegedly using drugs, including ganja, and informed the teachers. At their direction, he recorded videos of the alleged drug use and handed them over to the institution authorities.The teachers later visited the hostel and questioned the students, who reportedly admitted to using drugs. However, instead of taking further action, the teachers allegedly counselled them and let them go. The student was also asked to delete the videos, the complaint said.The classmates later realised that he had recorded the videos and reported them to the teachers. Three students allegedly abused and brutally assaulted him before locking him inside a room for the night.The following day, the student was admitted to a hospital after developing severe pain in his abdomen and genital area. As his condition worsened, he was shifted to Thiruvananthapuram Medical College Hospital, where doctors performed surgery and removed one of his testicles.The student initially did not tell his family about the assault, fearing reprisals. He informed his parents only on Aug 13, following which his father lodged a complaint with the Thodupuzha deputy superintendent of police.Police took one person into custody in connection with the incident. As he was a minor, he was produced before the Juvenile Justice Board and later released along with his parents.The victim’s family has sought action against the other two alleged assailants and demanded a detailed investigation into the incident.

Article Title: A Missouri engineer bought remote Ozarks land in 1970 and slowly built a reinforced-concrete home into the hillside; more than 50 years later, his son is restoring it room by room
Article Text:
Built into nature: The underground home was designed to blend seamlessly into the Missouri Ozarks hillside.

A home built into the Ozarks hillside

Designed to look like a natural cave

A cave-inspired entrance: A huge glass wall allows natural light into the home while creating the feel of a cave opening.

The underground home has its own natural ventilation system

Engineering underground: The house uses steel-reinforced concrete and an earth-based ventilation system to moderate temperatures.

From an Air Force missile silo to an underground home

A 58,000-pound railroad caboose sits on the property

A 58,000-pound relic: A vintage railroad caboose sits on the property after being transported and lifted into place with cranes.

Conway also built a homemade airboat

A homemade airboat powered by an aircraft engine

Zane Conway takes up the task of preserving his father’s unusual creation

An extraordinary underground home in Missouri’s Ozarks is offering viewers a rare glimpse into an unconventional experiment in architecture, engineering and sustainable living. Built by engineer Conway over several years, the house was carved into a hillside without an architect and with little outside assistance. Nearly five decades after construction began, the unusual residence reportedly remains leak-free.The underground house sits on a 225-acre property in the St. Francois Mountains of southeast Missouri. Conway bought the land in 1970 and began developing the property a few years later, gradually transforming the hillside into a home that was designed to blend into its natural surroundings.Conway’s son, Zane, recently gave unconventional homes expert Kirsten Dirksen a tour of the property in a YouTube video, explaining how his father spent years designing and constructing the house largely by himself.The project reflected Conway’s philosophy of building everything himself rather than purchasing conventional solutions. Zane recalled that his father believed that if he could not afford something, he would simply build it.“Everything fitting into nature, not overwhelming nature, but living in a symbiotic relation with nature,” Zane explained while describing his father’s vision for the property.Rather than constructing a conventional house and covering it with earth, Conway excavated deep into the hillside and built the structure into the natural grade. The home is protected by roughly a foot of steel-reinforced concrete, with several feet of earth above it.The entrance was deliberately designed to resemble the mouth of a cave. A huge glass wall allows natural light to enter the otherwise underground structure, while heavy oak beams and concrete columns create an interior that resembles a mine shaft.During the tour, Dirksen observed that the house feels like entering a mining shaft.That aesthetic was closely connected to Conway’s professional life. He worked in Missouri’s lead-mining industry and spent years developing his engineering skills in heavy industrial environments. His fascination with mining and railroads eventually became a defining part of the house’s design.One of the most striking aspects of the property is its ventilation system, which was incorporated into the design from the beginning.Air enters through a shaft located several feet away from the house and travels through the surrounding earth before reaching the interior. According to Zane, the system was designed to moderate the temperature of incoming air, helping cool it during summer and warm it during winter.The underground location also provides protection from extreme temperature fluctuations. The surrounding earth acts as a temperature moderator, allowing the interior to remain more stable than the outside environment.Each room has fresh-air vents, while exhaust fans in the bathroom and shower areas remove humid air from the house.The design demonstrates how passive strategies such as earth sheltering, natural ventilation, shading and thermal mass can reduce reliance on conventional heating and cooling systems.There may also have been another influence on Conway’s comfort with underground living.Before building the Missouri house, Conway served in the US Air Force and was part of a four-man crew working in Titan II missile silos. Zane said he has wondered whether his father’s experience living deep underground influenced the design, although Conway never confirmed that connection.The engineer’s approach to construction was consistent throughout his life: if he wanted something that did not already exist, he built it himself.Before the underground house, he had constructed a camper after returning from military service. He later built a large Quonset-style structure on the property before beginning the hillside home.The underground house is not the only unusual structure on the 225-acre property.Visitors are greeted by a vintage railroad caboose weighing approximately 58,000 pounds. Conway, who was an avid railroad enthusiast, acquired the decommissioned caboose in 1991 and had it transported to the property using cranes after separating its frame from the wheel trucks.The caboose remains largely in its original condition, with old railroad equipment, lanterns, paperwork and other details preserved inside. Conway had planned to eventually turn it into a guest home, although he never completed that project.His passion for railroads is also visible throughout the underground house, where kerosene railroad lanterns and mine-inspired details contribute to its distinctive character.Another unusual creation on the property is a homemade airboat powered by a Cessna aircraft engine.According to Zane, his parents built the fiberglass boat themselves. The project was another example of Conway’s tendency to create rather than buy, with the aircraft engine chosen for its ability to produce high torque at relatively low RPM.The property therefore became a collection of Conway’s engineering experiments, from the underground home and Quonset structure to the railroad caboose and homemade airboat.Conway died in 2018, and his son Zane has since taken on the task of maintaining and restoring the property and underground house, working on it room by room.For Zane, the house is more than an architectural curiosity. He grew up on the property and helped his father with the construction. One of the smaller bedrooms was his room as a teenager, and he still stays there when he visits.“This is my home,” Zane said during the tour, describing his emotional connection to the place.
Article Summary: The underground house sits on a 225-acre property in the St. Francois Mountains of southeast Missouri. Built by engineer Conway over several years, the house was carved into a hillside without an architect and with little outside assistance. The house uses steel-reinforced concrete and an earth-based ventilation system to moderate temperatures.

Article Title: Man walking his dog discovers a 3,400-year-old Bronze Age axe in an English forest
Article Text:
Image: Forestry England

A chance walk led to an extraordinary archaeological discovery

Researchers date the axe to between 1400 and 1275 B.C.E. Image: Forestry England

Researchers date the axe to between 1400 and 1275 B.C.E.

The Bronze Age transformed how prehistoric people made tools

How this 3,400-year-old axe offers a glimpse into ancient Britain

A routine walk through one of England’s ancient forests led to an extraordinary archaeological discovery when a man and his dog came across an axe head believed to be around 3,400 years old. What initially looked like an unremarkable object lying in the landscape was later identified as a relic from Britain’s Bronze Age, a period that transformed how prehistoric communities made tools, weapons and other objects. According to the BBC, researchers believe the axe dates from between 1400 B.C.E. and 1275 B.C.E. That places it within a crucial period of Britain’s prehistoric past, when communities were increasingly skilled at working with metal. The accidental discovery also demonstrates how ancient artefacts can remain concealed in familiar landscapes for thousands of years before resurfacing in the most unexpected circumstances. For archaeologists, the object offers a tangible connection to people who lived and worked in Britain more than three millennia ago.The discovery happened during an ordinary walk through an ancient English woodland, where the man was accompanied by his dog.While moving through the forest, he noticed an object that appeared unusual enough to investigate. What followed was the identification of an artefact that had survived from prehistoric Britain, making the casual find far more significant than it first appeared. According to the BBC, the axe head was eventually recognised as dating to the Bronze Age. Such discoveries are particularly valuable because archaeological evidence is often scattered across landscapes, with many objects remaining buried or hidden for centuries. The circumstances of this discovery also underline the unpredictable nature of archaeology. A simple walk can sometimes reveal evidence of human activity that predates recorded history by thousands of years, transforming an otherwise ordinary stretch of woodland into a place of archaeological interest.Researchers have dated the axe head to between 1400 B.C.E. and 1275 B.C.E., meaning it was made around 3,400 years ago. That places the object firmly in Britain’s Bronze Age, a time when the use of metal was becoming an important part of everyday life. The date also gives archaeologists a clearer idea of when the axe was made and used. It belongs to a period when Bronze Age communities were producing bronze objects for a range of purposes, including tools and weapons. As bronze is mainly created using copper and tin, this material represents a great progress from many stone implements which were invented before. It was possible to shape it in a number of ways and to create durable items, such as axes. These facts prove that there existed great skill of Bronze Age people in using metal.This axe gives an insight into the extent of technological advancement that occurred in Britain during the Bronze Age. Prior to the invention of bronze, tools were created from natural sources like stone, bones and woods. Metalworking enabled them to create better and more useful tools and weapons. Creating the bronze axe was quite an ordeal. People needed access to copper and tin, as well as the knowledge to heat, mix and shape the metals. The skills involved suggest that Bronze Age communities had developed a good understanding of metalworking and passed those techniques between generations. Because of this, the axe is more than just an old tool. It is evidence of the knowledge and craftsmanship that existed more than 3,000 years ago. Its discovery could also offer clues about how people used the surrounding landscape, although there is still no way to know exactly why the axe was left where it was found.The discovery shows just how much of Britain’s past can still be hiding in places people pass through every day. The axe had remained in the landscape for around 3,400 years, surviving changes in the environment until it was spotted during a routine walk. For archaeologists, findings such as these are a valuable source of information on how people used to live, work and make tools back in the Bronze Age. The identity of the owner of the axe, as well as reasons why the axe ended up being buried where it was discovered will probably remain a mystery; however, the type of material and its construction will provide some information on the time. This is also an example of how ancient history does not necessarily reveal itself in famous places of archaeological excavations. The finding could have been made in a forest, a field or a walkway. For the man and his dog, it was simply an unexpected find. For researchers, it is a small but fascinating piece of Britain’s Bronze Age story.
Article Summary: Researchers have dated the axe head to between 1400 and 1275 B.C.E. It belongs to a period when Bronze Age communities were producing bronze objects for a range of purposes, including tools and weapons. The axe had remained in the landscape for around 3,400 years, surviving changes in the environment until it was spotted during a routine walk.

Article Title: Archaeologists find earliest physical evidence of brass-making in East Asia in southern China
Article Text:
Archaeologists find the earliest physical evidence of brass-making in East Asia in southern China (PC: Cambridge University Press)

Ancient crucibles reveal early brass-making in medieval China

Ancient crucibles reveal early brass-making in medieval China (PC: AI Generated)

How did ancient craftspeople make brass from copper and zinc

How did brass-making technology reach medieval Guangzhou

What does the discovery reveal about medieval metallurgy in China

A set of ancient crucibles found in Guangzhou is giving archaeologists new clues about how brass-making technology may have reached medieval China. The vessels came from an official metallurgical workshop at the Royal Palace of the Nanyue Kingdom and dated from the ninth and tenth centuries AD. Their metal residues show that craftspeople were producing brass locally through cementation rather than simply working with imported objects. According to a research article published by Cambridge University Press, titled ‘ Brass technology transmission via maritime routes: crucible evidence from southern China ’, points towards wider technological connections with the Islamic world. Guangzhou was a major trading port, and the authors suggest maritime routes may have helped move metallurgical knowledge across regions. The study analysed crucibles using chemical, microscopic and lead-isotope methods. Together, the findings provide direct archaeological evidence for medieval brass production in southern China and offer clues about how the technology may have travelled.Archaeologists found three well-preserved brass-making crucibles at an official metallurgical workshop in Guangzhou. The workshop was part of the Royal Palace of the Nanyue Kingdom site and was active across many centuries.The three crucibles belong to the ninth–tenth century group. Each was cup-shaped with a slightly inward-sloping rim and a rounded base. Some had a pouring spout. They measured about 60-80 mm across and 60-70 mm high, with a capacity of roughly 0.2-0.3 litres. Researchers found heavy heat damage and glassy material on their surfaces. Metal residues inside included copper, zinc compounds and brass droplets. A nearby semi-subterranean furnace also dates to the seventh-tenth centuries. Together, these remains provide direct evidence of metalworking at the site.The crucial evidence came from residues left inside the crucibles. Microscopic and chemical analyses identified zinc oxide, zinc silicate, and droplets of brass. One group of crucibles contained high-purity copper and binary brass droplets with about 11-17% zinc. Another contained bronze with tin alongside zinc and produced a copper-zinc-tin alloy. The researchers interpret these residues as evidence for cementation. In this process, zinc-bearing material is heated with copper or a copper alloy so zinc enters the metal and forms brass. The remains therefore show more than the presence of finished brass objects. They preserve traces of the production process itself.The study also examined lead isotopes to investigate the likely origin of the raw materials. The three analysed crucibles had similar lead-isotope ratios that fit signatures associated with the Cathaysia tectonic province. Because these signatures occur widely across southern China, the researchers say a local source for the raw materials is reasonable. The technology itself may have travelled from farther west. The authors point to similarities between the Guangzhou crucibles and brass-making vessels associated with the Islamic world. Guangzhou was also a major international trading port. Historical evidence records connections between the city and Arab merchants. The researchers therefore suggest that maritime routes and the movement of merchants and craftsmen may have helped transmit brass-making knowledge to southern China.The findings add important evidence to the history of brass production in China. Local brass production is generally thought to have begun around the tenth century AD, but the Guangzhou crucibles provide direct evidence from the ninth-tenth centuries. The researchers argue that the discovery helps explain how a specialised metallurgical technique became established locally. It also shows why archaeological workshops can reveal details that written records alone cannot provide. The study does not claim that every element of brass technology came from one place or through one route. Instead, it highlights a possible connection between western technological traditions, maritime trade and local production in Guangzhou. The evidence adds an important piece to the history of metallurgy in East Asia.
Article Summary: Archaeologists found three well-preserved brass-making crucibles at an official metallurgical workshop in Guangzhou. The crucibles dated from the ninth and tenth centuries AD. Their metal residues show that craftspeople were producing brass locally through cementation rather than simply working with imported objects.

What the painted stone reveals about Austronesian expansion

A small painted stone found on Indonesia’s Wetar Island is offering archaeologists a glimpse into the symbolic world of ancient seafarers. It dates to about 4,090 to 3,900 years ago and features a red design of concentric circles and radiating sun rays that is linked to the Austronesian Painting Tradition (APT). The discovery is significant because the artwork was mainly known from cave and rockshelter walls. Research published in PNAS titled ‘4000-year-old painted plaque from Southeast Indonesia reveals Austronesian Painting Tradition preceded Neolithic pottery’ provides the earliest known example of the tradition.Researchers say it also changes the picture of what Austronesian voyagers carried as they moved between islands. Their journeys involved more than technologies, possessions and economic practices. Shared symbols and ideas may also have travelled with them, helping communities express identity, affiliation and beliefs during one of prehistory’s most extensive human dispersals.The painted plaque was discovered during excavations at Huknaur rockshelter on Wetar Island in Indonesia. It was recovered in situ from a transitional archaeological layer between Palaeolithic and Neolithic occupation.The stone carries a red design made of concentric circles and radiating lines, described as a sun-ray motif. Researchers identify this pattern as a characteristic of the Austronesian Painting Tradition, an artistic tradition found across eastern Indonesia and parts of the Western Pacific. Unlike most known APT paintings, which appear on cave or rockshelter walls, this example was made on a portable object. Its archaeological context is important because it provides a secure date for the motif and shows that APT imagery existed on movable objects and surfaces.Radiocarbon dating indicates that the plaque dates to between 4,090 and 3,900 calibrated years ago. This makes the object older than the first pottery found at the site. The plaque was discovered in a preceramic layer, showing that the Austronesian Painting Tradition was present on Wetar before pottery became a material marker used to trace Austronesian expansion. The researchers connect this early date with the movement of Austronesian-speaking peoples across Island Southeast Asia. The finding supports an early origin for the APT and suggests that symbolic traditions were already established during the earliest phases of maritime expansion, rather than emerging only during later periods of intensified inter-island contact. This gives archaeologists a clearer picture of early APT development.The portable nature of the plaque shows how ancient symbols travelled. A painting in a cave wall remains in one place, while a painted object can move with people from one island to another. The researchers suggest that portable symbols may have helped communicate shared identities, affiliations and beliefs between communities. Similar sun-like designs were historically painted on boats and other objects, where they could serve as symbols of protection and group identity.The plaque does not prove exactly how this particular design was used, but its existence shows that APT imagery was not limited to rock surfaces. It provides material evidence that symbolic expression could make art a part of the traditions carried by maritime communities widely. The finding therefore adds another dimension to understanding how cultural ideas may have travelled alongside people during ancient ocean voyages.The Austronesian dispersal was a major human migration in prehistory, with descendants of populations associated with Taiwan eventually reaching islands across a vast area, from Madagascar to Rapa Nui. At the site, the plaque was found in a frontier layer that lacked typical Austronesian ceramics but contained novel elements, including bead types associated with Austronesians.The researchers argue that ideology may have been important at the wavefront of expansion. The plaque points to a movement in which people carried not only practical knowledge and possessions, but also shared artistic traditions and symbolic ideas widely.

It dates to about 4,090 to 3,900 years ago and features a red design of concentric circles and radiating sun rays that is linked to the Austronesian Painting Tradition.

Article Title: In the 1970s, one New Mexico architect began building homes from discarded tyres and cans; his Earthship idea is now being adapted for extreme weather
Article Text:
PC: Earthship Biotecture

How Michael Reynolds turned discarded tyres, cans and bottles into Earthship homes

PC: Image AI generated

What are the six defining elements of an Earthship home

How Earthship homes were used after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami

Why Earthship homes have faced building code and planning restrictions

Why Earthship ideas are becoming relevant beyond homes built with tyres and cans

In the New Mexico desert, discarded car tyres, beer cans and bottles became the unlikely foundations of a different kind of home. Architect Michael Reynolds began developing his Earthship idea in the early 1970s, turning waste materials into thick walls designed to hold heat and houses built to produce and manage many of their own basic needs. For decades, the strange-looking buildings remained a niche experiment, often running into planning rules and scepticism. Now the idea is being viewed through a different lens. As hurricanes, floods, tornadoes and power failures leave conventional homes cut off from essential services, Earthships are attracting renewed attention for their ability to operate independently of the grid. What began as an experiment in using rubbish has gradually become a model for thinking about how homes might cope when the infrastructure around them stops working.Reynolds began developing the idea in the early 1970s in New Mexico, after becoming dissatisfied with the limits of conventional architectural practice. His early experiments involved materials that had little obvious place in a building. Beer cans, bottles and discarded tyres became part of the construction rather than waste to be removed. The approach eventually developed into what Reynolds called the Earthship, a type of passive-solar home built around recycled materials and systems intended to reduce dependence on outside utilities.The Financial Times, writing about Reynolds' work in the documentary Garbage Warrior, described his use of recycled cans, plastic bottles and earth-filled car tyres in houses designed to need little or no heating even during New Mexico's severe winters.The tyres were not simply being used because they were available. Filled with compacted earth, they became part of the heavy walls, giving the buildings considerable thermal mass. That allowed the houses to store and gradually release heat rather than relying entirely on conventional heating and cooling equipment. An early house known as the Thumb House, built in 1972, is described in material accompanying Garbage Warrior as an early example of Reynolds' use of discarded glass and plastic, tin cans and earth-filled tyres, alongside systems for handling heat, water and sewage.The idea was a long way from mainstream housing. For years, Reynolds' early Earthships attracted little interest, with some of the first structures sitting empty. That changed gradually. According to NBC News, structures based on the concept have since been built in 35 US states as well as internationally. The same report notes that the houses are constructed with at least 40 per cent recycled material and are designed to use roughly one-sixth the power of a conventional home.An Earthship is not defined simply by having tyres in its walls. Reynolds' system brings several separate functions together inside the same building. His six defining elements include the use of natural and repurposed materials, passive or solar heating and cooling, electricity from solar and wind power, rainwater collection and reuse, contained sewage treatment, and the ability to grow food on site.That changes the relationship between a house and the infrastructure outside it. Rain falling on the roof, for example, does not necessarily leave the property as runoff. Collected rainwater can first be used for activities such as washing before passing through filtration systems, after which it can be used for toilets and plants. The basic principle is simple: a resource enters the building, is used more than once where possible, and is dealt with on site rather than depending entirely on a municipal network.The same thinking applies to electricity. Solar panels and, where suitable, wind generation are intended to supply power without a conventional connection to the grid. The result is a home designed to remain operational even when the wider utility network is unavailable. That does not mean every Earthship is identical or completely independent in practice. Owners can choose how closely they follow the full model, and this flexibility has attracted criticism from people who question whether a house should be called fully sustainable if it adopts only some of the principles.The idea became clearer when Reynolds' work moved beyond the desert. After the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, his team travelled to the Andaman Islands in 2005 to work with communities dealing with the destruction left behind. The project was not a theoretical exercise. Local people needed buildings, materials were limited, and the normal processes of development were hardly suited to the circumstances. Architect Nileshe had discovered Reynolds' work and invited him and his team to construct a demonstration building in the islands.The experience also showed why a building's independence from central infrastructure could matter after a disaster. Reynolds and his crew constructed low-tech shelters in the aftermath of the tsunami using local materials and ideas drawn from the Earthship communities in New Mexico. The work offered a practical setting for methods that had spent years being tested in a very different environment.That history now sits alongside a newer interest in Earthships as disaster-resilient housing. Reynolds' company had begun working in places affected by tornadoes and hurricanes, including southeastern Kentucky and Puerto Rico. The report also linked the renewed attention to events such as the 2021 Texas winter storms, when widespread power failures left households without electricity for days.The attraction is not difficult to understand. A conventional house may remain physically intact after a storm but become difficult to live in if electricity, water or sewage systems are knocked out. An Earthship attempts to keep several of those functions inside the building itself. The structures are designed to be more resistant to hurricanes, tornadoes and floods and can function as emergency shelter while remaining independent of a damaged power grid.Reynolds' work has never fitted comfortably into ordinary planning systems. The same features that make an Earthship unusual also create regulatory problems. Conventional building codes tend to assume a house will connect to established electricity, water and sewage networks and will use familiar construction materials. Reynolds' houses were deliberately designed around a different arrangement. His buildings therefore became entangled in disputes with authorities in New Mexico, including battles over licences, planning rules and whether experimental communities could operate outside standard requirements.That tension has not disappeared simply because interest in self-sufficient housing has grown. According to the Earthship Academy, students attending have reportedly travelled from different countries to learn about solar and wind systems, water management and indoor food production; practical lessons do not automatically translate into permission to build an Earthship anywhere. The case of a student who wanted to construct one but faced restrictions in Illinois over some of the materials used in the structures. An architect from Belgium attending the same course said he was interested in applying individual Earthship ideas to conventional buildings rather than necessarily reproducing the entire model.That may be where the concept is becoming more relevant. The future of Earthship design does not necessarily depend on every new house being built from tyres and cans in the same form Reynolds developed in New Mexico. Parts of the system can be separated from the distinctive architecture: generating some household electricity on site, capturing rainwater, reducing heating and cooling demand, reusing materials and creating ways to continue operating when external services are interrupted. In that sense, the old New Mexico experiment is being treated less as a fixed house design and more as a collection of building ideas.The shift is a subtle one. Reynolds began by questioning why architecture needed to rely so heavily on conventional materials and centralised services. Decades later, the same question has acquired a practical edge in communities facing hurricanes, floods, tornadoes and prolonged power outages. The Earthship was never designed simply as a response to extreme weather; its emphasis on thermal stability, renewable energy, water reuse and independence from utility networks has given the old experiment context.

For decades, the strange-looking buildings remained a niche experiment, often running into planning rules and scepticism. Now the idea is being viewed through a different lens.

Article Title: A Kansas couple is building a tornado-resistant home from 1,000 tyres, 16,000 cans and 1,000 cardboard boxes; construction begins this year
Article Text:
Image: Earthship's official site

A home where waste becomes part of the structure

Designed to withstand Kansas' extreme weather (Image: Earthship's official site)

Designed to withstand Kansas' extreme weather

An off-grid system built around energy, water and waste

What the Kansas Earthship says about future housing

A Kansas couple is turning thousands of discarded everyday objects into an unusual home designed for a region where extreme weather can arrive with little warning. Their Earthship incorporates about 1,000 tyres, 16,000 aluminium cans and 1,000 cardboard boxes, transforming materials that would ordinarily enter waste streams into components of a functioning house. The residence is part of the Earthship movement founded by architect Michael Reynolds and is built around the idea that a home can provide more than shelter. It can generate electricity, collect rainwater, manage wastewater, regulate indoor temperatures and support food production. The Kansas project is particularly notable because it is a tornado- and fire-resistant Refuge Earthship, combining recycled-material construction with structural features intended for extreme weather. According to Earthship Biotecture , the special Kansas ground-up build is scheduled for September 14 to October 8, 2026, giving participants the chance to watch the home take shape from the ground up.The most striking feature of the Kansas house is its material list. Rather than relying exclusively on conventional bricks, blocks and other manufactured building products, the Earthship approach incorporates discarded materials directly into the construction. The roughly 1,000 tyres are used as part of the structural wall system, while thousands of aluminium cans and cardboard boxes are incorporated elsewhere in the build.This is not simply a visual statement about recycling. Earthship Biotecture describes its buildings as being made from natural and upcycled materials, with around half of an Earthship constructed from recycled or upcycled materials. Tyres are particularly useful because they can be packed tightly with earth, creating massive walls with substantial thermal mass. Those walls can absorb heat and release it gradually, helping stabilise indoor temperatures and reducing dependence on conventional heating and cooling. The cans and other reclaimed materials similarly become part of a building system that treats waste as a potential resource rather than something that must immediately be removed from the site.The Kansas project goes beyond the usual image of an off-grid sustainable home because resilience to severe weather is central to its design. Earthship Biotecture identifies the Kansas build as a new fire- and tornado-resistant Earthship, with the structure incorporating four ferro-cement vaults. These are thin-shell structural elements made from cement mortar reinforced with steel wire mesh and rods, forming part of the home's protective architecture. The design reflects the reality that sustainability alone does not make a building resilient: a house also needs to withstand the environmental conditions of the place where it stands. In Kansas, that means accounting for powerful storms and tornadoes as well as fire. The Earthship concept approaches that challenge by combining heavy earthen construction, passive thermal design and specialised structural elements rather than treating disaster protection as an entirely separate feature. The result is intended to function as an ordinary residence while also offering a more robust refuge during extreme conditions. The specific tornado performance of the Kansas residence should, however, be understood as a property of this engineered project rather than proof that every Earthship is automatically tornado-proof.The unusual construction materials are only one part of what makes an Earthship different from a conventional house. Earthship Biotecture describes the design around interconnected systems for electricity, water, thermal comfort, wastewater and food production. Solar photovoltaic panels generate electricity, while rain and snow can be collected and stored in cisterns. The organisation also uses systems that treat and reuse greywater on site, reducing reliance on conventional water and sewage infrastructure. Thermal mass is another crucial component: dense walls help keep interiors warmer during colder periods and cooler during hotter ones, potentially reducing the need for conventional energy-intensive climate control. Food production is incorporated through indoor growing areas, making the building itself part of the household's resource system. A 2026 paper titled ‘ Earthship- The future sustainable house ’ published in Interactions by Raja Sekhar Mamillapalli and colleagues similarly examined Earthships as sustainable, self-sufficient housing, highlighting their thermal envelope, renewable-energy systems, water harvesting and water-reuse systems. The researchers concluded that Earthships can represent a financially feasible housing alternative in semi-arid climates, although that study concerns the broader Earthship model rather than specifically validating the tornado resistance of the Kansas residence.The completed Kansas home ultimately represents a broader experiment in how houses could respond to two problems at once: growing material waste and increasingly demanding environmental conditions. Its tyres, cans and cardboard are reminders that construction does not always have to begin with newly manufactured materials, while its solar power, water collection, wastewater treatment and thermal-mass design challenge the assumption that a comfortable home must remain heavily dependent on external infrastructure. That combination is at the heart of the Earthship philosophy. Earthship Biotecture describes its houses as buildings intended to address six human needs, including shelter, energy, water, sewage treatment, food production and waste management. The Springer research adds an academic perspective to that approach, describing Earthships as homes designed to provide occupants with essential amenities while reducing dependence on public connections. The Kansas residence takes those ideas into a region where resilience is especially important. Instead of simply building a conventional house and adding a storm shelter, the project brings structural protection, reclaimed materials and autonomous systems together in one design. Its most important lesson may therefore be less about living inside a house made from tyres and cans, and more about reconsidering what a house can do: shelter its occupants, produce some of its own resources, reuse what society throws away and remain better prepared for a world in which extreme weather and infrastructure disruptions are becoming harder to ignore.
Article Summary: The Earthship is part of the Earthship movement founded by architect Michael Reynolds and is built around the idea that a home can provide more than shelter. It can generate electricity, collect rainwater, manage wastewater, regulate indoor temperatures and support food production. The Kansas project is particularly notable because it is a tornado- and fire-resistant Earthship.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

Legal validity of Jeevan Pramaan



How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.
Article Summary: Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.

Hassabis, a Nobel Prize recipient, will take the newly created title of Alphabet’s chief scientist and transition from being Google DeepMind CEO to being its chairman, he said in a memo to staff.Koray Kavukcuoglu, the unit’s chief technology officer, will assume day-to-day responsibilities of DeepMind in addition to his parallel role as Alphabet’s chief AI architect.

Article Title: Google Pixel 11 Pro XL first impressions
Article Text:
Design and security

Performance

Gemini Intelligence now works ahead of you

Magic Capture for that perfect click

Camera Looks lets you choose your own style

Creator Suite simplifies content creation

Instant Night Sight speeds up low-light shots

Live Translate breaks language barriers instantly

What we think

Google’s newest flagship, the Pixel 11 Pro XL, has landed, and it comes packed with a fresh set of upgrades built around Gemini Intelligence and a reworked camera system that is supported by computational photography. From smarter photo sensors to an assistant that proactively steps in before you even ask, this year’s phone is clearly aimed at making everyday tasks simpler rather than bringing about notable changes in the hardware. Sure, the Pixel 11 Pro XL (price starting at Rs 1,34,999) packs improved security and processor upgrades, but those specs are tough to measure solely by benchmarks. Google’s true focus with this lineup is giving users a device that minimises screen time so you can actually focus on real life. Here's a look at everything that is new.The Pixel 11 Pro builds on Google’s refined aesthetic that has remained largely unchanged since the Pixel 9 Pro XL. The phone gets a brighter 6.8-inch Super Actua display than its predecessor. It features the same sleek, flat glass-and-metal sandwich design with Gorilla Glass Victus 2 and an IP68 rating. The phone retains the iconic horizontal rear camera bar, which has been cosmetically refined.The Pixel 11 Pro XL debuts HiLight, which works as an enhanced indicator light. Its functions are limited for now. The visor now has a full glass covering.The Pixel 11 Pro XL is powered by Tensor G6, which is claimed to offer better AI performance and handle daily tasks proactively. The phone gets a bunch of AI-driven features that are made possible by the new Tensor G6 chip, which handles the heavy lifting for on-device generative AI tasks like live dubbing and translation, letting the phone process complex features quickly without needing to lean entirely on the cloud. Add to that Titan M3, which adds a layer of intelligent security. Google says that the chip is capable of providing security from quantum attacks.The idea of the Pixel 11 Pro XL is not to perform well in raw benchmarks but to offer an experience that minimises human effort. For example, your friend recommends a restaurant that you also like. Now instead of searching for it and making a booking, Gemini will proactively offer you a reservation, which can be done in fewer taps. Here are a few AI features coming in the Pixel 11 Pro XL.The biggest shift with the Pixel 11 Pro XL is how much more capable Gemini has become at handling tasks on your behalf. It can now string together multiple steps across more than 40 apps and counting, and several of these abilities are debuting on Pixel before anywhere else.Google Pixel phones have been leaders for point-and-shoot photography, and with Gemini on Pixel 11 Pro, things are getting a bit easier. Magic Capture is built to catch those fleeting shots automatically that you may miss if you are a split second late.Not everyone loves the same photo aesthetic, and Camera Looks acknowledges this by allowing you to select your preferred style at the moment you take the shot. While the classic Pixel look remains a favourite for many, Google now offers three new default options: Natural, which keeps details relaxed; Shadows, which adds deeper contrast; and Vanilla, which brings a warm, golden tone. If you want to go further with personalisation, there are six additional Looks to choose from: Digi, Black Tie, Minimal, Editorial, Classic, and Velvet.For anyone who films content regularly, the new Creator Suite is designed to remove friction from the process. It brings an on-screen teleprompter that scrolls in sync with your speech, so you never lose your place while recording.If you have used Pixel smartphones in the past, you know how much time it takes for the phone to capture a shot in low-light condition. Google is fixing this by reducing time. Google says Night Sight shots can now be captured up to 4.5 times faster than before. During our time with the phone, it did speed up those times, helping us not to hold still for ages just to get a great low-light photo.Live Translate brings real-time translation to videos and audio as they play. It relies on real-time speech-to-speech translation, powered by advanced on-device generative AI models running on Google's Tensor G6 chip, automatically dubbing content from other languages into the one you prefer.Our early impressions are that Google Pixel 11 Pro XL has evolved into more of an experiential phone that offers a mix of great photography, clean software with straightforward design, and loads of AI features that aim to make day-to-day things easier for users over time. Tensor G6 still lags behind most of the flagship chipsets, but Google, like always, is aiming for a more software-centric approach rather than a hardware-led offering. We’ll talk about more in our full review.
Article Summary: Google’s newest flagship, the Pixel 11 Pro XL, has landed. It comes packed with a fresh set of upgrades built around Gemini Intelligence. From smarter photo sensors to an assistant that proactively steps in before you even ask, the phone is clearly aimed at making everyday tasks simpler rather than bringing about notable changes in the hardware.

Article Title: Sekyo Carepal Pro 2026 review: Safety, calling and GPS tracking in one watch
Article Text:
Display and design

Performance

Verdict

The Sekyo CarePro PAL 2026 is a kids' safety smartwatch (as the company calls it) that aims to combine communication, location tracking and safety features in one device. Listed at Rs 5,780 on the company’s website, it is positioned as more than a basic smartwatch, with features such as 4G calling, live GPS tracking, SOS alerts, Safe Zone notifications and parent-controlled monitoring. It also includes educational games and routine reminders for children. On paper, the CarePro PAL 2026 looks like a device designed to give parents more control while giving children some independence. But the real question is whether all these features work together well enough to make the Rs 5,880 price worthwhile in everyday use.Sekyo CarePro PAL 2026 has a design that feels clearly made for children rather than trying to look like a miniature version of an adult smartwatch. In our daily use, we found it comfortable enough for a child to wear throughout the day, while the compact form factor made it easy to use for calls, location checks and other basic functions.The watch also comes with a selfie camera, which adds to its practical appeal for children. We could use it for basic photos and video calling, while parents can access some of the camera-related features through the Sekyo app.The smartwatch has a 1.44-inch LCD display with a resolution of 240 x 240p.The display is primarily focused on usability rather than offering the kind of high-end screen experience we see on premium smartwatches. In our use, it was adequate for checking notifications, navigating the watch, making calls and accessing the games and other features. The touchscreen also makes it easier for children to interact with the device without relying on a smartphone.In our use, the 4G connectivity on the Sekyo CarePro PAL 2026 was central to the experience, as it allowed us to make HD video calls, phone calls and voice chats without giving the child a smartphone. Parents can also restrict communication to approved contacts, which adds an important layer of control.With Raksha Bandhan in mind, this is where the watch can also make sense as a gift from one sibling to another. Instead of being just another gadget, it can be a practical way for parents to stay connected with a younger brother or sister while allowing them some independence.We found the live GPS tracking to be one of the more useful features for parents. The Sekyo app can show the child's location, route history and step count. Parents can also create a Safe Zone, with an alert sent when the child moves outside the defined area.The SOS button adds another safety feature. A single press can share the child's live location and call up to three trusted contacts. For parents, this can provide an additional way to respond quickly when a child needs help.The watch also offers remote controls through the Sekyo app. We could enable school mode, block calls from unknown numbers, locate the watch and remotely disable or switch it off.The CarePro PAL 2026 comes with seven educational and maths games, along with an alarm, phone book and selfie camera. Routine reminders for activities such as brushing, homework, reading and bedtime can also help children follow a daily schedule.At Rs 5,880, the Sekyo CarePro PAL 2026 is aimed at parents who want to give a child some independence without handing over a smartphone. Its 4G calling, live GPS tracking, SOS alerts, Safe Zone notifications and parental controls make it more focused on safety and communication than typical kids' smartwatches. The educational games and habit reminders also give children something to use beyond calling and tracking. However, parents should remember that features such as GPS tracking and remote monitoring are dependent on connectivity and the companion app, so the overall experience can vary in real-world use.At Rs 5,880, the CarePro PAL 2026 makes the most sense for families that will actually use its safety and communication features. For a Raksha Bandhan gift, it offers a practical way to keep a younger brother or sister connected while giving parents greater peace of mind.
Article Summary: Sekyo CarePro PAL 2026 is a kids' safety smartwatch that aims to combine communication, location tracking and safety features in one device. It has features such as 4G calling, live GPS tracking, SOS alerts, Safe Zone notifications and parent-controlled monitoring. The smartwatch has a 1.44-inch LCD display with a resolution of 240 x 240p.
